text_en: In recent years, the spread of the internet has let anyone obtain vast amounts of information instantly. It goes without saying that this is convenient, but it has also created problems we cannot ignore. People tend to gather only information that matches their own views, and their chances to encounter different opinions are shrinking. What is more, systems that select information based on browsing history are accelerating this tendency. Even experts find it hard to escape this influence entirely. The problem lies not in the amount of information but in how we handle it. Precisely because we live in an age overflowing with information, we need the ability to check sources and think from several standpoints. Schools, too, should not only make students memorise knowledge but emphasise training in reading information critically. In the end, whether technological progress is put to good use or wasted depends on the judgement of the people who use it.

text_en: This study was conducted to clarify how sleep affects memory consolidation. Participants were sixty university students, all of whom memorised the same word list. Half were then allowed eight hours of sleep, while the other half stayed awake all night. In a test the next day, the group that slept averaged 78% correct, whereas the group that did not sleep reached only 52%. This gap was almost constant regardless of word difficulty. These results suggest that sleep works to organise and consolidate memories. However, the study covered only young people, so the same result may not hold for older adults. The fact that it was carried out in the special setting of a laboratory should also be considered when interpreting the results. Going forward, we plan to study a wide range of age groups under conditions closer to everyday life.

text_en: In the alley at dusk, the smell of grilling fish drifted from somewhere. A wind chime hanging from the eaves rang softly, as if it had suddenly remembered to. The paving stones still held the heat of the day and softly received the footsteps of children running barefoot. In contrast to the bustle beyond the station, where high-rise buildings stood in rows, here even time seemed to flow slowly. I stopped in front of a weathered wooden signboard. The ink-brushed characters had almost faded, but I did not need to read them to know it was the name of the shop my grandfather had run. Peering through a gap in the door, I saw the evening sun slanting onto dusty shelves. The days when, as a small child, I had watched my grandfather's hands at work in front of these shelves without ever tiring came back as if they were yesterday. I could not hold back the nostalgia welling up from deep in my chest. Far off, the tofu seller's horn sounded, and the alley slowly took on the colours of night.
